title: Yom Kippur: one long blast
hookLine: Neilah ends with a single long shofar note and "next year in Jerusalem"

cards: The sun is going down. Nearly a full day without food or water. People who've been sitting stand up, because the ark has been opened, and it will stay open for the whole last service.
Many stand for all of it. Legs ache. Voices are hoarse.
Some who went home at midday are back, and the room fills up again for this hour. The service has a name that sounds like a door swinging shut.

teach.h: NEILAH: THE CLOSING OF THE GATES.
teach.b: It's called Neilah, the closing, or the locking. The ancient sources debate what's being closed. One view: the gates of the Temple, locked at the end of the day.
Another: the gates of heaven, closing as the day ends. Either way, the image is a gate, still open, just barely. The words change.
All through the ten days, the prayers asked: write us in the book of life. Now, in Neilah, they ask: seal us. Chotmenu.
Write becomes seal. The service builds, and at the very end comes a sequence everyone knows. The congregation says the Shema's first line once.
Then blessed be the name of His glorious kingdom, three times, out loud, the line usually whispered.

Then a verse from Elijah's contest on Mount Carmel, when the people saw fire fall from heaven and cried out: "The LORD, He is God; the LORD, He is God." It's said seven times, louder each time. And then the shofar.
Not the long sets of Rosh Hashanah: one single, long blast, a tekiah gedolah, held as long as the blower's breath will last. Everyone answers together: l'shanah haba'ah b'Yerushalayim.
Next year in Jerusalem. It's an odd way to end.
Not we did it, or we're forgiven, but hope pointed forward: a long sound that doesn't break, and a promise about next year. Then people go home and eat.

how: The Neilah service closes Yom Kippur with the ark open throughout; it ends with the Shema, 'Baruch shem' three times, 'The LORD, He is God' seven times, a single long shofar blast and 'next year in Jerusalem.'

games.q: the sun has set at the end of Yom Kippur. the shofar sounds one long note. what does the congregation call out?
games.why: l'shanah haba'ah b'Yerushalayim: the day ends with hope pointed forward.

practice: Think of something that's ending soon, a day, a week, a project, even a hard chapter, and picture its last moment with a forward-pointing line to close it: next time, next year, I'll be back.
Breathe in, then let out one long breath, the longest you can, like the last shofar note; if you pray, let that breath carry a hope to God.
